etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English communicacion, from Old French communicacion, from Latin commūnicātiōnem, accusative singular of commūnicātiō (“imparting, communicating”), from commūnicō (“I share, I impart”). Morphologically communicate +‎ -ion.

definitions.definition: The act or fact of communicating anything; transmission.
(uncountable) The concept or state of exchanging data or information between entities.
A message; the essential data transferred in an act of communication.
The body of all data transferred to one or both parties during an act of communication.
An instance of information transfer; a conversation or discourse.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:

definitions.definition: A passageway or opening between two locations; connection.

quote.citation: 1727, John Arbuthnot, Tables of Ancient Coins, Weights and Measures. Explain'd and exemplify'd in several dissertations:
quote.text: The Euxine Sea is conveniently situated for trade, by the communication it has both with Asia and Europe.

quote.citation: 1900, Patents for Inventions: Abridgments of Specifications, page 75:
quote.text: This communication between the tank and pump is controlled by a float valve in the tanks and a cock in the pipe, while a poppet valve prevents the undrawn liquor going into the waste tank.

definitions.definition: (anatomy) A connection between two tissues, organs, or cavities.

quote.citation: 1855, William Stokes, The Diseases of the Heart and the Aorta Page 617
quote.text: ...and here a free communication had been established between the aorta and the vena cava.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Bible Corinthians/#15 1 Corinthians:15–33:

quote.text: We admit them in the Church to a right of Communication to drink of the Cup of the Bloud of Christ.

definitions.definition: (rhetoric) A trope by which a speaker assumes that his hearer is a partner in his sentiments, and says "we" instead of "I" or "you".

quote.citation: 1798, James Beattie, Elements of Moral Science:
quote.text: Communication […] takes place when a speaker or writer assumes his hearer or reader as a partner in his sentiments and discourse, saying We, instead of I or Ye.
